title: A Language for the Interior
premise: Jude Okafor, a restaurant critic whose palate died with his mother, has built a life of polished distance—until Amara Diallo, the last fluent speaker of Kɛlɛn, a dying language of her river town, insists he become her final student. As Jude learns words for things English has no names for—grief that arrives early, joy that costs something—he is pulled into Amara's estranged family and a land dispute in which a developer is erasing her village's history with legal precision. When Amara's health fails faster than his lessons, Jude must choose between the invisibility that has protected him and speaking, publicly and in Kɛlɛn, at the hearing that will decide the village's fate. He loses the land but keeps the language, and in teaching it to Amara's granddaughter, he finally tastes food again.
about_author: Yara Marchetti is a former translator who spent a decade documenting endangered oral traditions across West Africa before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted fishing hut in Portugal, where she keeps a notebook of untranslatable words she refuses to define.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A scathing review, a numb tongue, and a funeral he attends only for the catering establish his armor: charm as a locked door. When a letter arrives requesting 'one final student' for a dying language, he almost files it away. Emotional beat: the first crack in his practiced indifference, disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: Words for Water That Has Already Passed
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. He visits Amara Diallo, ninety-one and sharp as broken glass, expecting to decline politely. Instead she assigns him homework: learn ten words for the river's moods. He cannot pronounce a single one, and she refuses to translate. Emotional beat: humiliation that feels, strangely, like being seen.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Goodbye
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. We learn Kɛlɛn has no future tense—only the near-now and the already-gone—and that Amara has buried two children and a language. She chose Jude not for his talent but because his obituaries mourn food he can no longer taste; she recognizes a man grieving in advance. Emotional beat: recognition between two people fluent in loss.

chapters.title: A Table With Too Many Chairs
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Amara drags him to a family dinner with her estranged granddaughter Naya, a lawyer representing the developer threatening the village's river rights. Jude, hired palate, recognizes the caterer's fraud; Naya recognizes her grandmother's new student as a liability. Emotional beat: found family forming inside an argument, everyone armed with different languages.

chapters.title: What the River Owes
chapters.summary: Naya's POV. Naya's brief reveals the developer's case is built on a falsified 1970s land survey—and that her own firm buried the original. She visits Amara to warn her and leaves with a recording of a lullaby she hasn't heard since childhood. Emotional beat: the law she trusted begins to feel like a dialect of betrayal.

chapters.title: Ten Words for Hunger
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Amara collapses mid-lesson; a stroke takes her English first, leaving Kɛlɛn intact. Jude, now her only conversation partner in it, must translate her doctors, her jokes, her anger. He cooks for her from his old reviews and, for one spoonful, tastes salt. Emotional beat: language becoming a lifeline; the critic's palate flickering back to life.

chapters.title: The Inheritance of Silence
chapters.summary: Amara's POV, fragmenting. Slipping between tenses, Amara recalls the residential school where Kɛlɛn was beaten out of her generation, and why she let her own children go untaught. She entrusts Jude with her recordings—not as archive but as obligation. Emotional beat: guilt transmuted at last into a bequest; the weight of being a last speaker lifted onto another.

chapters.title: Everything the Survey Erased
chapters.summary: Naya's POV. Naya finds the original survey in her firm's cold storage and faces disbarment if she discloses it. She brings it to Jude, not Amara, and asks him what their grandmother would want. Jude answers in Kɛlɛn—the first full sentence he's ever spoken aloud. Emotional beat: the found family choosing each other over safety.

chapters.title: The Near-Now
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. At the land hearing, Amara, wheelchair-bound and English-less, cannot testify—so Jude stands and speaks her statement in Kɛlɛn, translating the falsified survey's human cost into the record, his voice breaking on the word for 'home that is being already-gone.' The developer wins on a technicality; the room hears everything anyway. Emotional beat: climax—justice outside the law, spoken in a language the law cannot touch.

chapters.title: A Language for the Interior
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, then Naya's. Amara dies in the near-now she always taught, and Jude delivers the eulogy in Kɛlɛn. He resigns from criticism, opens a small school with Naya—now disbarred, now free—and cooks a meal from his mother's recipe, tasting every bite. Emotional beat: resolution—goodbye said properly, out loud, and a language that will outlive its last speaker.
